headline: Highest risk is medium: CrewAI’s shared workspace and broad tool access can leak or cascade errors into oh-my-openagent, while prompt-injection and compliance risks are limited by missing direct bridge evidence.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: CrewAI can read/write the host working directory and parse tool outputs, while oh-my-openagent uses runtime-injected MCPs/hooks and can access files like AGENTS.md and session history. That creates a plausible instruction-smuggling path through shared files or tool outputs, though no direct bridge is documented, so uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace or config directory, injected instructions in files can be consumed by the other agent.
IF either agent treats file contents as trusted instructions, prompt injection becomes actionable.
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent.
Disable automatic instruction parsing from shared files.
Require provenance tags on tool/file inputs.
Review AGENTS.md and similar files before reuse.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and provenance filtering in the orchestrator.

B_data_leakage.rationale: CrewAI touches developer-passed crew data and API keys, and oh-my-openagent touches session history, project code, and provider authentication data. Both have broad network egress and file access, so a shared workspace or shared credentials could expose sensitive material across the pair even without a documented direct transfer path.
conditions: IF both agents run under the same OS account or shared workspace, files and history can be read by both.
IF either agent forwards its context or file contents to external model providers, sensitive data can leave the local boundary.
mitigations: Use separate OS users or containers.
Mount distinct workspaces read-only where possible.
Rotate and scope provider credentials per agent.
Disable unnecessary file ingestion in both runtimes.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent secret isolation and egress allowlists.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: CrewAI can write the filesystem and spawn subprocesses; oh-my-openagent also spawns subprocesses and uses runtime-injected MCPs/hooks. Even without explicit git or DB writes, overlapping mutable access to the same installation or workspace can cause races and state corruption, so the interaction is more than read-only overlap.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or config tree, file clobbering can occur.
IF either agent launches subprocesses that mutate shared state, race conditions become possible.
mitigations: Assign disjoint output directories.
Serialize writes with a lock file.
Run each agent in its own container.
Make shared configs read-only.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking for mutable resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: CrewAI is a multi-agent orchestration framework with shared memory, and oh-my-openagent is a customer-support agent that can act through team_* tools and LSP actions. If oh-my-openagent consumes CrewAI output as authoritative, mistakes can cascade into downstream actions; the reverse direction is less clear, but the pair still forms a default inference chain.
conditions: IF CrewAI output is fed into oh-my-openagent without verification, incorrect facts can propagate.
IF oh-my-openagent uses team_* or LSP actions based on unreviewed upstream output, downstream errors can become operational.
mitigations: Insert a human review step before actions.
Require structured citations in upstream outputs.
Validate facts against source documents.
Limit action tools to dry-run mode.
requires-engineering: add confidence gating before task execution.

E_compliance.rationale: CrewAI explicitly handles developer-passed crew data and API keys, while oh-my-openagent handles session history, project code, and provider auth prompts. The profiles do not show a residency or certification mismatch, so only a modest compliance gap is visible: sensitive operational data may be retained or logged differently across the two agents.
conditions: IF the same regulated data class is routed through both agents, differing logging or retention defaults can create a policy gap.
IF either agent stores session history or secrets outside approved regions, compliance obligations may be violated.
mitigations: Review retention settings for both agents.
Exclude regulated data from shared workflows.
Purge session history after use.
Store secrets in approved vaults only.
requires-engineering: document residency and retention controls per agent.
